2.5.       Membrane setup and operating conditions Experiments were run using a LabStak M20 filtration device from Alfa Laval, France (Fig. 2) allowing several flat-sheet membranes to be tested simultaneously. Each tested membrane has a separate permeate outlet. The retentate outlet is common for all membranes. The effective area for each membrane was 2 x 0.018 m^2 and the initial wastewater feed volume was approximately 30 L. The feed tank and main parts of the pilot were of stainless steel in order to limit artefact adsorption. [SOURCE: Page_134]

Fig. 2- Scheme of the LabStak M20 system (Sagne et al. 2008) [SOURCE: Page_134]

A new membrane was used for each experiment, which consists of three steps: deionized water filtration for 2 hours maximum, then wastewater filtration for 4 hours maximum, and finally (after rinsing) deionized water filtration again. For all experiments, retentate flow-rate was set at 300 L.h-1; temperature was kept constant at 20°C (jacketed tank); and Trans- Membrane Pressure (TMP) was increased incrementally from 5 to 30 bar (5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 bar). The experiments were run in total recirculation mode: both permeate and retentate were recycled into the feed tank. Sampling and measurements were made after a minimum filtration time of 10 min. Filtration tests with deionized water were conducted to determine the permeability of pure water (A in L.h-1.m-2.bar-1) of the membrane before and after wastewater filtration. According to Darcy’s law, pure water flux (Jw in L.h-1.m-2) is proportional to TMP (in bar) according to: [SOURCE: Page_134]

𝐽 = 𝐴 × 𝑇𝑀𝑃                                                                                  (1) ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    105 [SOURCE: Page_134]

𝐽 =                                                                                         (2) 𝑇𝑀𝑃 =               −𝑃                                                                      (3) [SOURCE: Page_135]

With: Qp            Permeate flow rate (L.h-1) experimentally established by plotting. S             Effective membrane area (m^2) Pf, Pr and Pp Feed, retentate and permeate pressures, respectively (bar). [SOURCE: Page_135]

Filtrations were performed on solutions in order to study the influence of TMP on permeate flux and solutes (COD, sugars, ions) rejections. ### 3. Results and Discussion

3.1.       Characteristics of raw wastewater Table 3 sums up the detailed composition of the processing plant's drinking water and of the different effluents. Composition of the wastewaters strongly varies over time, with COD values lying between 22 and 4730 mg O$_2$.L-1. This is consistent with a report from the European Union (2018) which identified a COD variation between 18 and 5402 mg O$_2$.L-1 in effluents from fruit and vegetable industries. [SOURCE: Page_136]

### 3.1.1. Wastewater from the peeling machine

For wastewater from the peeling machine, Lehto et al. (2014) measured a COD between 9.0 and 39.0 g.L-1 which is significantly higher than the present values and can be explained by the abrasive and machine peeling mode used in their study. Furthermore, the wastewater studied here is a mix of peeling and rinsing water. Wastewater from the peeling operation is gathered in the condensed stream from the initial peeling step, but wastewater from the subsequent rinsing is also collected, resulting in average temperatures of up to 31°C. It contains TSS (peelings), dissolved substances such as sugars (fructose, glucose and sucrose) and ions including mainly chlorides, sulphates, sodium, potassium and calcium (Table 3). Sugars are the major identified compounds and represent between 36 and 67% of the total COD and between 51 and 92% in its dissolved form. With CODtot/BOD$_5$ = 2.1, this effluent is therefore highly biodegradable (Truc, 2007). Studies are underway to more accurately identify the additional dissolved substances, especially peptides and amino acids present in carrots and detected by UV spectrophotometry in the effluent (OD215 between 2 and 2.5). According to the USDA Nutrient Database, glutamic acid, threonine, aspartic acid, alanine, leucine and lysine, with molecular weights between 80 and 150 g.mol-1, are the main amino acids present in carrots. No pesticides were detected, probably because carrot roots are less exposed than their above-ground parts; they could also have been eliminated with residual soil during the cleaning process. [SOURCE: Page_136]

### 3.1.2. Wastewater from the blanching operation

Wastewater from the blanching operation contains the same components as the peeling wastewater, but at higher concentrations. Blanching consists of bringing the carrots to a high temperature for a short period of time in order to inactivate or retard bacterial growth and enzyme action. It uses hot water at 80°C to 100°C, or steam, and leads to wastewater temperatures between 64°C and 71°C. This results in an increase in sugars solubility and diffusion (more than 40% for sucrose between 30°C and 65°C) (Macedo, 2005) and explains their higher concentration and COD levels. ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    107 [SOURCE: Page_136]

### 3.1.3. Selection of key parameters and other indicators

In order to identify the origin of the compounds in the effluent, the composition of wastewater was compared to that from standard carrot-processing procedures, as well as with drinking water from the processing plant (Table 3). Higher concentrations of minerals in wastewater confirm their transfer from carrots during peeling. For instance, wastewater contains up to 95 mg.L-1 of K+, whereas drinking water contains only 4 mg.L-1; this can be explained by the elevated presence of this element in carrots: 320 mg/100 g. With respect to sugars, equivalent amounts of fructose and glucose are found in carrots, while the level of sucrose is 8 times as high. In the wastewater produced, the proportions of fructose and glucose are respected, and even if its presence is 8 times that of fructose and glucose, it would appear that sucrose tends to transfer to a much lesser extent. A possible explanation could be hydrolysis into fructose and glucose. According to the methodology developed in the ANR MINIMEAU to reduce water consumption, key parameters (specific compounds to be eliminated) have to be selected (Garnier, Guiga, Lameloise, Degrand, et al., 2019). The production of water of drinking quality requires the elimination of TSS and the reduction of the COD figures. Fructose, glucose and sucrose are the major components of this effluent and may provoke rapid bacterial growth. As disinfection of wastewater is a priority in the fruit and vegetable industries (Manzocco et al., 2015), their removal constitutes a primary objective. TSS, COD, fructose, glucose and sucrose were therefore chosen as key parameters. As mineral concentrations are lower in the wastewater than those found in drinking water, they do not appear as key parameters for the treatment process evaluation, but they represent essential indicators that have to be monitored at each step of the treatment scheme. In fact, it was shown that they can affect the rejection rate of organic solutes through modification of membrane properties (pore swelling, electrical charge, etc.) or even through the molecular radius of the different solutes (Galier, Savignac, & Roux-de Balmann, 2013; Mohammad, Basha, & Leo, 2010). Moreover, with respect to pH and CH control, they provide an overview of the water's state of equilibrium, and thus a basis for evaluating the risk of scaling or corrosion. For example, scaling near the membrane can cause fouling (Aimar et al., 2010). [SOURCE: Page_137]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_140]

3.2.       Pre-treatment selection Pre-treatment operations were selected to comply with manufacturers’ recommendations regarding the maximal SDI. Particles contained in peeling effluents settle very quickly (in less than 2 min), which leads to a reduction in COD of around 22%. In fact, in the EU (European, 2018a), the largest particles from peeling are generally separated by sedimentation. In this study, sedimentation was replaced by an equivalent sieving step, utilising microfiltration. Rapid fouling was observed via SDI tests with the filtrate after sieving from 169 µm to 30 µm. This is consistent with the particle size analysis of this effluent, revealing a particle size distribution in volume mainly between 30 µm and 2000 µm and a D43 of about 600 µm (Table 4). These results agreed with those of Nelson et al. (2007) with particle size lying between 0.5 and 1000 µm for fresh cut-vegetable wastewater (shredded lettuce, raw vegetable salad, peeled baby carrots and other vegetables). SDI was reduced to 17 after MF at 1.6 µm and less than 5 after further filtration at 0.5 µm. It appears essential to micro-filter the effluent at 0.5 µm prior to further treatment. [SOURCE: Page_140]

Table 4: Example of particle size distribution after several pre-treatments [SOURCE: Page_140]

Wastewater          Wastewater          Wastewater Raw pre-treated at      pre-treated at      pre-treated at wastewater 169 µm               79 µm              0.5 µm D43 (µm)               591                 194                 108                 n.d. D32 (µm)               148                  60                  47                 n.d. n.d.: not determined [SOURCE: Page_140]

Progressive sieving at 169, 79 µm and dead-end MF at 0.5 µm were then applied as pre- treatment. Sieving leads to a decrease in D43 at successively 194 µm and 108 µm. The removal efficiency of this pre-treatment reaches 93% for TSS (89% by sieving at 169 µm) and an average of 28% for COD (26% at 169 µm). COD reduction is lower but consistent with that obtained by Reimann (2002) (between 30 and 40%), where pre-treatment was pushed towards ultrafiltration with a pore diameter of 0.05 or 0.1 µm. The pre-treated effluent was analysed for its residual pollution: 1 - 52 mg.L-1 TSS, 16 - 3 406 mg O$_2$.L-1 COD 50 - 930 µS.cm-1 conductivity, 1 - 151 mg.L-1 fructose, 0 - 187 mg.L-1 glucose and 10 - 663 mg.L-1 sucrose. [SOURCE: Page_140]

3.3.       Membrane water permeability Before wastewater treatment, pure water permeability of the selected membranes was studied (Fig. 3). A high linear correlation (r^2 > 0.991) between the pure water permeate flux and the TMP was found according to Darcy’s law and equation (see equation 1, above). Resulting water permeability values are given in Table 5. [SOURCE: Page_140]

Fig. 3 - Pure water permeate flux (20°C, feed flow rate=300 L.h-1): (a) NF membranes and (b) RO membranes. [SOURCE: Page_141]

Values of water permeability are consistent with those reported by other authors (Table 5) except for the NFW membrane. Variations in water permeability may be due to differences in filtration module geometry or in compaction procedures (Mohammad et al., 2010; N. Nguyen et al., 2016). As expected, RO membranes display lower water permeability than NF, with the exception of the ESPA$_4$ (RO) which has higher permeability than the DK (NF). Amongst RO membranes, the ESPA$_4$ exhibits the highest permeability followed by the BW30 and the HRX whereas for the NF membranes, the NF270 exhibits the highest and the DK the lowest permeability. [SOURCE: Page_141]

3.4.       Critical flux, concentration polarization and fouling In what follows, “solution” will refer to the pre-treated effluent tested utilising NF or RO. Pure water permeability at 20°C was measured before and after solution treatment, and the corresponding loss of permeability was calculated to evaluate potential fouling (Table 5). Whatever the membrane type, when pure water permeability was initially higher than 4 L.h-1.m-2.bar-1, a loss of water permeability up to 23% was found, showing that with these membranes, fouling had occurred. Permeate flux for the solution was also measured and compared with initial pure water flux. Two different behaviours were observed: for the less permeable BW30 (Fig. 4) and HRX membranes, the relation between permeate flux and TMP was linear, showing that the critical flux was not reached in this range (Aimar, 2006; Bacchin, Aimar, & Field, 2006). The DK membrane displayed quite the same behaviour, but only up to 25 bar. Permeate flux was always below that of pure water, with a gap increasing along with TMP, corresponding to a pressure gap of up to 5 bar for the highest fluxes. This highlights a reversible concentration polarization phenomenon (Aimar et al., 2010), not taken into account in these figures: in fact, sugars and salts in the solution are responsible for an osmotic pressure of only 0.16 bar (eq. 7), which could in no way explain the pressure gaps observed (Fig. 4, 6 and 7). This phenomenon was also mentioned by (Almazán, Romero-Dondiz, Rajal, & Castro-Vidaurre, 2015) during the nanofiltration of glucose: introducing concentration polarization into the calculation of osmotic pressure to correct TMP (eq. 4), they observed that both permeate and pure water fluxes curves merged. For membranes with the highest permeability (above 4 L.h-1.m-2) such as the NFW (Fig. 5), the linearity range was reduced as water permeability increased: it was linear up to 20 bar for the ESPA$_4$ and only 5 bar for the NF270. When the critical flux is exceeded, irreversible fouling occurs, as was previously observed by the permeability loss of these membranes (Table 5). [SOURCE: Page_143]

For the ESPA4 (Fig. 6) and the SR3D (Fig. 7) membranes (with water permeability of 6.3 and 7.5 L.h-1.m-2.bar-1, respectively), the evolution of permeate flux was studied over time to check critical flux value. For each pressure applied up to 20 bar, two flux measurements were ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    115 [SOURCE: Page_144]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_145]

made, after 5 min (initial flux) and after 30 min of the run; for 30 bar, it was measured after 5, 15 and 30 min. At the lowest pressures, no permeate flux difference was observed with time, showing that no fouling had occurred and that the steady state was quickly reached. For both membranes the same critical flux of about 80 L.h-1.m-2 was reached at TMP = 18 bar for the ESPA$_4$ and TMP = 15 bar for the SR3D, above which permeate flux decreased with time. A decrease of up to 15% for the highest TMP was observed after a 30 min run. This confirms the result of Reimann (2002) who showed that for RO membrane, flux stabilization occurred only after several hours of run. When the pressure was further decreased (from 30 bar to 1 bar), hysteresis appeared for both membranes, consistent with the fact that the critical flow had been exceeded (Aimar et al., 2010). Fouling phenomena did not depend on the type of membrane (NF or RO), but rather on water permeability level. As RO membranes are dense membranes, irreversible fouling probably develops on the outer surface of all the membranes tested. A more efficient pre- treatment would not solve fouling problems as shown by Reimann (2002) for an equivalent effluent (low-contaminated washing water for carrots): with ultrafiltration with a 0.1 µm or 0.05 µm pore diameter as pre-treatment, a loss of permeate flux during the first two hours of RO treatment was also observed. Both concentration polarization and fouling phenomena may have either beneficial or detrimental impacts on membrane selectivity (Aimar et al., 2010). Consequently, membrane performances were compared before and after the critical flux. [SOURCE: Page_145]

3.5.        Sorption phenomena Adsorption can increase with polarization concentration and impact fouling (Aimar et al., 2016). To assess sorption phenomena, an experiment was run on the LabStak M20 device equipped with 3 pairs of membranes (total filtration area = 0.108 m^2) and without TMP (TMP = 0 bar). The initial volume in the tank was 28.1 L. Samples were taken in the tank at the beginning and after 30 min of operation, when equilibrium was expected to be reached. As expected for a microfiltrated solution, there is no more difference between total and dissolved COD. Results (Table 6) show a loss of fructose, glucose and sucrose of, respectively, 5 mg.L-1, 4.8 mg.L-1 and 23 mg.L-1, probably due to adsorption on the membranes. It corresponds to a calculated CODsugars loss of 36 mg O$_2$.L-1 while COD loss is about 88 mg O$_2$.L-1, showing that other molecules (equivalent to a CODdiff of about 52 mg O$_2$.L-1) such as peptides are also adsorbed on the membranes. Actually, proteins have a strong tendency to adsorb on membranes (Aimar et al., 2016). The quantity adsorbed is about 1.3 g.m-2 for fructose, 1.3 g.m-2 for glucose and 6 g. m-2 for sucrose. Such adsorption had already been observed by Nguyen et al. (2016) for glucose, but at a lower level. No significant discrepancy is noticed in ion concentrations before and after contact with the membranes. [SOURCE: Page_146]

3.6.          COD and sugars rejection The rejection of COD and sugars versus permeate flux for NF membranes are given in Fig. 8. They increase with the solute MW and decrease with the MWCO of the membrane (Table 2) indicating that size exclusion is the major mechanism for the studied solutes tested on these membranes. This conclusion is consistent with other studies (Mohammad et al., 2010; N. Nguyen et al., 2015). The maximal COD rejections for the DK (150-300 g.mol-1), the NF270 (150 -300 g.mol-1), the SR3D (200 g.mol-1) and the NFW (300-500 g.mol-1) membranes are, respectively, 95.8%, 94.9%, 92.1% and 82.8% (Fig. 8-a) and correspond to minimal COD values in the permeate of, respectively, 20, 25, 48 and 82 mg O2.L-1. The same membrane ranking is observed with sugars (Fig. 8-b and -c), the most rejected being sucrose, which the highest MW. Due to their equivalent chemical structure, MW and Stokes diameter, there is no significant difference between glucose and fructose in terms of rejection, whatever the membrane. Nevertheless, glucose rejection is always slightly higher than that of fructose. Such phenomena had already been observed between two C5 sugars and attributed to hydration differences (Galema & Hoeiland, 1991; Hua, Zhao, Yang, Zhang, & Zhao, 2010; N. Nguyen et al., 2015). It could also be explained by differences in the interaction energy with the membrane, as suggested by ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                     118 [SOURCE: Page_147]

(Yao et al., 2018) for the rejection of monosaccharides in NF membranes. It is also observed that rejections decrease when the permeate flux increases above the critical flux (between 80 and 100 L. h-1.m-2 for all the membranes), as already noticed to a lesser extent for glucose in a model mixture by Nguyen et al. (2015) with the NF270 membrane and for the highest flux (above 150 L.h-1.m-2). To the contrary, Almazán et al. (2015) who studied glucose behaviour alone in solution, observed a stabilisation of its rejection for increasing pressure and for different membranes including the DK. Then, for a complex solution such as carrot-peeling wastewater, working above the critical flux has a negative impact on the rejection of sugars. [SOURCE: Page_148]

Fig. 8 – Rejection of COD and sugars as a function of permeate flux with NF membranes (20°C, feed flow rate=300 L.h-1): (a) COD, (b) glucose and fructose, (c) sucrose. [SOURCE: Page_148]

Regarding RO, whatever the membrane, the permeates contain between 10 and 17 mg O$_2$.L-1 corresponding to a COD rejection of about 97.2% ± 0.9% (Figure not shown). At the same time, fructose, glucose and sucrose rejections are about 99.2% ± 0.5%. Whatever the pressure, COD and the rejection of sugars are always high due to a predominant size exclusion effect. This is consistent with other studies on sugars, always rejected at more than 95% (N. Nguyen et al., 2015). Given this high rejection range, no difference can be made between sucrose and C$_6$ sugars, and a fortiori between glucose and fructose. The fact that the rejection of COD is always inferior to the rejection of sugars suggests that [SOURCE: Page_148]

additional (and not quantified) organic solutes in the solution pass through the membrane more easily than sugars. This is confirmed by the calculation of CODdiff rejection for two NF (DK and NFW) (Fig 9-a) and two RO (BW30 and ESPA$_4$) membranes (Fig 9-b). It appears always slightly below COD rejection, confirming that these solutes are less rejected than sugars. For treatment with the ESPA$_4$, OD215 rejection was only about 92% ± 3%, similar to CODdiff rejection showing that these solutes could be amino acids. [SOURCE: Page_149]

3.7.        Rejection of minerals Rejections of monovalent and divalent ions are presented separately. Due to their quasi absence in the raw wastewater (Table 3), nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+) rejection figures are not presented, as is the case for the only trivalent ion detected (PO43-), which is always 100% rejected regardless of membrane type. Figure 10 shows rejections obtained for monovalent ions (Na+, K+, Cl-) with the four NF membranes. The rejection order between the membranes is in accordance with MgSO4 rejection indicated by manufacturers (Table 2): higher for the SR3D (MgSO4 rejection > 99%) followed by the DK (MgSO4 rejection 98%), NF270 (MgSO4 rejection 97%) and the NFW (MgSO4 rejection 97%). The same tendency was observed for divalent ions (Ca2+, Mg2+, SO42-) in Fig. 11. An exception was observed with the SR3D membrane for magnesium (Fig. 11-b) and sulphates (Fig. 11-c), highlighting a different behaviour for this membrane. This is consistent with the measures of pH (Table 7), CH (Table 8) and OD215 of the permeate: indeed, pH and CH are much lower as compared with other membranes, suggesting a higher migration of protons and a lower migration of bicarbonates (HCO3-, major form at neutral pH). At the same time, OD215 rejection is smaller, at 31% ± 9% showing that the transfer of amino acid type molecules though this membrane is much higher. The rejections of monovalent ions (Na+, K+, Cl-) (Fig. 10) were globally lower than that for divalent ions (Ca2+, Mg2+, SO42-) (Fig. 11), lower than that of the trivalent PO43- (100%). As an example, rejection rates for Na+ and Mg2+ (40% and > 90% respectively) are very different ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                     120 [SOURCE: Page_149]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_150]

for DK membrane at 60.L.h-1.m-2, although they have similar MW. This is consistent with the Donnan space charge model (Aimar, 2006). For SO42- and PO43-, with higher, similar molecular weights (about 95 g.mol-1), the size effect is of major importance on their rejection, which moreover is not affected by the flux (no decrease above the critical flux). Rejection values for sulphates were 100% for the DK and the NF270, 97.2% for the NFW and 96.3% for the SR3D, consistent with manufacturers’ data (Table 2) with the exception again of the SR3D which displays lesser sulphate rejection than expected, perhaps balanced by higher bicarbonate rejection, as noticed above. Regarding magnesium, for all the membranes, the maximal rejections are significantly lower than expected: 93.6% for the DK, 82.0% for the NF270, 59.3% for the NFW and 88.4% for the SR3D. This could be explained by the presence in the effluent of additional non-qualified small negatively charged molecules. Indeed, the ionic mass balance indicates that the sum of the negatively charged ions is lower than that of the positively charged ions charges (example for the DK membrane at 5 bar in Table 9). This difference is greater for the retentate, showing that those negatively charged molecules are well retained (76%). As shown previously (OD at about 215 nm), the presence in wastewater of amino acids such as glutamic acid, aspartic acid and lysine is suspected. Being negatively charged at neutral pH (Table 10), they would transfer together with cationic molecules or minerals, such as magnesium ions to ensure electroneutrality, which might explain its unexpected lower presence. [SOURCE: Page_150]

3.8.    Choice of NF or RO membranes for the reconditioning treatment Amongst NF membranes, the NF270 at TMP = 15 bar appears as the best compromise in terms of COD rejection and permeate flux. Nevertheless, at this pressure, the permeate flux is above the critical value which increases cleaning constraints. The DK membrane at the same TMP allows the same COD rejection to be obtained, but with a permeate flux below the critical flux. The corresponding permeate qualities are summarized in Table 12. For RO membranes, considering that COD rejection is not a relevant criterion here, the choice may be driven by the permeate productivity, and consequently the highest water permeability (Table 5). In that case, the ESPA$_4$ appears as the best choice, even more so it operates below the critical flux (TMP < 15 bar). The permeate quality with this membrane at a TMP of 10 and 15 bar is summarized in Table 12 and corresponds to rejections up to 98.3, 98.0, 99.2, 99.2 and 99.4% in conductivity, COD, fructose, glucose and sucrose, respectively. For the same operating pressure (TMP = 15 bar), the permeate produced with the ESPA$_4$ seems to most closely match the quality criteria for drinking water, with a much lower organic matter content (COD) especially, as compared with the DK and the NF270. Moreover, it has a similar productivity to the DK. For these reasons, and in order to have the best COD rejection while limiting the fouling risks, the ESPA$_4$ can be selected for complementary tests on a pre-industrial pilot scale. However, with the RO membrane's high conductivity rejection, particular attention would have to be paid to the calco-carbonic balance of the water produced in order to avoid corrosion. 4. Conclusions The production of water of sufficient quality for reuse in the vegetable industry was studied in the specific case of a complex carrot-peeling effluent. A pre-treatment consisting of double sieving steps at 169 µm and 79 µm, followed by a 0.5 µm microfiltration, was necessary to eliminate larger particles and minimize fouling issues for subsequent treatment steps. High-quality water with low conductivity (< 8 µS.cm-1), low COD (< 12 mg O$_2$.L-1) and low sugars content (< 4 mg.L-1) can be obtained by reverse osmosis treatment with the ESPA$_4$ membrane (Hydranautics-Nitto Group Company). As wastewater from blanching operations contains the same components as peeling wastewater, similar treatment could be considered and performances predicted. They allow for serious consideration of the possibility of water reuse in vegetable processing plants, prior to the blanching step which can act as a thermal barrier and further contribute to microbiological safety. However, water treated by reverse osmosis is demineralized, disrupting the calco-carbonic equilibrium and thus increasing the risks of corrosion. These issues remain to be studied on an industrial scale. [SOURCE: Page_155]

The CTCPA (Paris, France) is acknowledged for sharing its expertise in vegetable industries and for providing the industrial partner for the effluent supply. [SOURCE: Page_155]

PUBLICATION 3: Treatment of cauliflower processing wastewater by nanofiltration and reverse osmosis in view of recycling Céline GARNIER, Wafa GUIGA, Marie-Laure LAMELOISE, Laure DEGRAND and Claire FARGUES [SOURCE: Page_156]

Journal of Food Engineering DOI: 10.1016/ j.jfoodeng.2021.110863 [SOURCE: Page_156]

Keywords Membrane process, food industry, water reuse, effluent treatment, cauliflower, reverse osmosis [SOURCE: Page_156]

Abstract The vegetable industry is a large consumer of drinking water. This paper investigates the possibilities of Reverse Osmosis (RO) or tight Nanofiltration (NF) for the treatment of cauliflower blanching wastewater with a view to recycling within the production unit. Ultrafiltration at 100 000 g.mol-1 molecular weight cut-off was necessary to decrease turbidity below 1 NTU as required before NF or RO. Three NF (DK, NF270 and SRD$_3$) and one RO (ESPA$_4$) membranes were tested at bench-scale in a crossflow filtration mode. Only RO allowed to reach the desired quality for a reuse purpose, with an acceptable residual COD content of 225 mg O$_2$.L-1. The Solution-Diffusion model was validated for the transfer of glucose and fructose, for NF270, DK and ESPA$_4$ membranes and their permeability coefficients calculated. [SOURCE: Page_156]

Highlights: -   Ultrafiltration followed by reverse osmosis allows to consider recycling of cauliflower wastewater -   ESPA$_4$ membrane at 19 bar leads to 70 L.h-1.m-2 permeate flux and 95% COD rejection -   Solution-diffusion model considering concentration polarization was successfully applied -   DK, NF270 and ESPA$_4$ permeabilities for fructose and glucose were determined -   Nanofiltration with 150-300 g.mol-1 Molecular Weight Cut-Off is not suitable, due to the transfer of small metabolites [SOURCE: Page_156]

1. Introduction The industries that consume large amount of water are more and more keenly concerned by the necessity to save the water resources. The food industry, including the fruit and vegetable transformation sector, is particularly concerned: according to a study of the European Commission (European, 2018b), water consumption in the latter ranges from 0.5 to 15 m^3/ton of processed raw material. Reuse (recycling without treatment) and reconditioning (recycling after treatment) of these effluents thus become consequential in order to reduce the environmental impact of these industries and restore water quality to an acceptable level. [SOURCE: Page_157]

Considered as robust, flexible and “green” (Dewettinck & Le, 2011; Guiga & Lameloise, 2019), membrane processes are becoming favourite technologies for treating wastewater before recycling (Warsinger et al., 2018; Wenten & Khoiruddin, 2016) especially for the food processing industry (Meneses et al., 2017). Among them, reverse osmosis (RO) or tight nanofiltration (NF) ensure the highest water quality and have already proved valuable for wastewater reconditioning in the dairy (Bortoluzzi et al., 2017; Brião et al., 2019; Suàrez et al., 2014) and brewery industries (Braeken et al., 2004). They can provide high permeate fluxes and rejections at relatively low transmembrane pressure (TMP) provided several issues are considered: first, adequate pre-treatment should be implemented to bring the Silt Density Index (SDI) to below 5 and turbidity to 1 NTU (Sim et al., 2018). Second, membrane operations should be run below the critical flux to avoid irreversible fouling (Aimar et al., 2010). [SOURCE: Page_157]

The possibilities of reuse and reconditioning of wastewater in the food industry, and the development of toolboxes to evaluate the impact of these solutions are primary objectives in the French research program MINIMEAU (ANR-17-CE10-0015). A recent study on carrot peeling wastewater highlighted that high-quality water could be obtained through RO or tight NF membranes after microfiltration (MF) (Garnier et al., 2020). In the vegetable- processing industry, one plant usually transforms different vegetables, either simultaneously or successively. Consequently, the present study aimed to check the feasibility of the process developed in Garnier et al. (2020) for wastewater arising from rinsing of carrots after peeling, for treating wastewater from cauliflower blanching. [SOURCE: Page_157]

In the Drinking Water Standard, lists of parameters are to be respected for both drinking water quality and the water source from which it originates (mainly surface or groundwater), while there is no regulatory context outlining the water quality of recycled industrial wastewater. For food safety, drinking water is usually requested in the food processing industry (Casani et al., 2005). In this work, characterisation of the cauliflower blanching wastewater was made in order to select key parameters to be eliminated. Optimized pre- treatment and membrane treatment, convenient for both vegetable’s applications were [SOURCE: Page_157]

________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    128 [SOURCE: Page_157]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_158]

selected with drinking water quality as the objective. Finally, the Solution-Diffusion model, commonly used to represent water and solutes transfer in non-porous membranes (Qasim et al., 2019; Wijmans & Baker, 1995) was applied to obtain water and solutes permeabilities for NF and RO membranes, considering the concentration polarization phenomenon. In this work, it was acquired especially for sugars contained in cauliflower effluent, and compared with data extracted from the literature results. Such database is essential for the design tool developed in the MINIMEAU Project. [SOURCE: Page_158]

### 2. Material and Methods

2.1.       Wastewater origins The wastewater was obtained from the French factory already selected by the Technical Center for Food Product Conservation (CTCPA, Paris, France) for the study of Garnier et al. (2020) on carrot processing wastewater. This factory produces several frozen vegetables sometimes on the same production line. Effluents of cauliflower processing are produced at the outlet of several operation units. In particular, a cleaning unit is used only for cauliflower and a blanching and freezing unit alternately for all vegetables (Fig. 1). Blanching consists in a short heat treatment with hot water (80 °C to 100 °C) to inactivate or delay bacterial growth and enzyme action. Cauliflower wastewater collected at the outlet of the blanching operation unit was selected for our study and stored at -18 °C before treatment tests. Drinking water used in the factory was analysed as a reference. [SOURCE: Page_158]

Common units [SOURCE: Page_158]

Fig. 1. Schematic representation of vegetable processing operation in the factory under study. [SOURCE: Page_158]

________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    129 [SOURCE: Page_158]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_159]

2.2.       Analytical methods The following analyses were performed: - Global parameters: Total Suspended Solids (TSS), particulate and dissolved Carbon Oxygen Demand (COD), conductivity, pH, turbidity, Carbonate Hardness (CH), Total Nitrogen (TN), optical density, color, - Dissolved organic pollution: glucose, fructose (accuracy ± 4%) and sucrose (accuracy ± 5%), - Free and total chlorine (accuracy ± 0.06 mg.L-1 Cl$_2$), - Ionic composition: chloride, nitrite, nitrate, phosphate, sulphate, sodium, ammonium, potassium, magnesium and calcium (accuracy ± 2.5%). [SOURCE: Page_159]

Most analytical methods are already described in Garnier et al. (2020). High-performance ion-exchange chromatography (HPIC) was used to analyse anions and cations as well as sugars. At the pH of the effluent (4.7) and based on the equilibrium diagram of CO$_2$, the concentration of carbonate in the effluent was negligible meaning that Carbonate Hardness (CH) could represent the concentration of bicarbonate. COD (accuracy ± 3%), TN, CH (variable accuracy), chlorine (free and total) were determined with rapid test tubes and photometric measurement (Nanocolor vis II - Macherey Nagel, Hoerdt, France). Color and turbidity (accuracy ± 2%) were performed with the same photometric material. Color was established in the CIELAB color space adopted by the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) in 1976, where color is expressed as three values: L* (lightness from black (0) to white (100)), a* (from green to red) and b* (from blue to yellow). COD being mainly composed of sugars, additional organic matter was quantified through a differential COD (mg O$_2$.L-1) defined as: [SOURCE: Page_159]

CODdiff = COD − COD                                                                         (1) [SOURCE: Page_159]

Where CODsugars is the COD (mg O$_2$.L-1) deduced from sugars’ concentrations. and the stoichiometry of the oxidation reaction (1g.L-1 of fructose and glucose corresponds to a COD of 1.066 mg O$_2$.L-1 when 1 g.L-1 of sucrose corresponds to a COD of 1.122 mg O$_2$.L-1). UV absorbance measurement at 216.4 nm (OD216.4) and 264.4 nm (OD264.4) allowed evaluating the presence of amino acids or peptides. Samples were diluted ten times. [SOURCE: Page_159]

2.3.       Pre-treatment Sieving at 169 µm and 79 µm followed by dead-end MF 0.6 µm was first implemented, as in Garnier et al. (2020). The obtained turbidity remaining too high to fulfil quality requirements for further NF or RO step, the permeate obtained from MF was further ultra-filtrated. Three UF organic membranes with different Molecular Weight Cut-Off (MWCO), namely 100 000, 10 000 and 5 000 g.mol-1, were tested therefore (Table 1). [SOURCE: Page_159]

________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    130 [SOURCE: Page_159]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_160]

2.4.       NF and RO membranes Cauliflower processing wastewater contained sucrose (MW = 342 g.mol-1) and mainly glucose and fructose (MW = 180.16 g.mol-1). Consequently, three NF membranes with MWCO between 150 and 300 g.mol-1 and one RO membrane were selected for further purification (Table 1). New membranes were stored dry at 4 °C. To remove the protective coating or storage solution, they were dipped before experiments in a 0.4 g.L-1 KOH solution for 2 h and then in deionized water for 24 h minimum. Prior to experiments, membranes were pre-compacted (20 bar, 15 min) in the filtration device. [SOURCE: Page_160]

________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    131 [SOURCE: Page_160]

2.5.             Membrane setup and operating conditions Experiments were run using the LabStak M20 filtration device from Alfa Laval described in Garnier et al. (2020). It allows testing several flat-sheet membranes simultaneously. The effective area for each membrane was 2 x 0.018 m^2. [SOURCE: Page_162]

To study water permeability and solutes’ rejection, experiments were run in total recirculation mode: deionized water filtration (< 2 h) for pure water permeability measurement, wastewater filtration (< 8 h), and deionized water once more (after rinsing with deionized water for 10 min minimum). For all experiments, retentate flowrate was set at 300 L.h-1 and temperature at 20 °C. For UF membranes, two transmembrane pressures (TMP) were tested: 3 and 5 bar. For NF and RO membranes, TMP was increased from 5 to 25 bar by 5 bar steps and then decreased symmetrically. Sampling and measurements were done after at least 30 min run. [SOURCE: Page_162]

Once UF membrane selection was made, filtration was run in discontinuous mode to produce a sufficient amount of ultra-filtrated permeate: the permeate stream was collected in a distinct tank and the concentrate returned to the feed tank until reaching the desired volume reduction ratio (VRR): [SOURCE: Page_162]

### 4. Results and Discussion

4.1.       Characterisation of raw wastewater Cauliflower processing wastewater had a particular odour which could be attributed to sulphur and N-bearing molecules, and foaming attested the presence of proteins. Table 2 shows the composition of the blanching wastewater (two samples). The difference between total and dissolved COD (± 3%) was within the accuracy limit. [SOURCE: Page_164]

Fructose and glucose represented respectively 72% and 46% of the total COD of the raw wastewater, showing its variability. These proportions increased to 99% and 79% when raw wastewater was micro filtrated, indicating that these are the main dissolved organic substances present. Other organic dissolved substances were estimated by UV spectrophotometry at 216.4 nm (possibly corresponding to peptide bonds) and 264.4 nm (corresponding to aromatic rings), as well as by TN measurement. These may be amino acids or peptides/proteins possibly containing aromatic rings like histidine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and tyrosine, present in cauliflowers. [SOURCE: Page_164]

By comparing the composition of wastewater with that of typical cauliflower (Table 2), the transfer of sugars and most minerals (phosphate, sulphate, sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium) into wastewater during blanching is confirmed. Glucose and fructose are transferred in the same proportion. Sucrose, present in small amount in cauliflower (Bhandari & Kwak, 2015) is also transferred into the wastewater. [SOURCE: Page_164]

As in the study on carrot wastewater (Garnier, Guiga, Lameloise, Bertrand, et al., 2019; Garnier et al., 2020), TSS, COD, conductivity, fructose, glucose and sucrose were selected as key parameters. Concerning the French drinking water standard and regarding ions, only ammonium was out of the range (8–12 mg.L-1 in raw wastewater vs 0.1 mg.L-1 in French standard), so it was selected as another key parameter. The other ions were merged as key parameter “conductivity”. As raw wastewater was white with an orange tint, color was also monitored. [SOURCE: Page_164]

4.2.            Pre-treatment selection The removal efficiency of the sieving-MF pre-treatment was 60% for TSS, 34% for COD, 17% for OD216.4, 39% for OD264.4 and null for sugars. Nevertheless, the residual turbidity (average 48 NTU) was too high for feeding a NF or RO process. Additional pre-treatment with UF membrane (MWCO of 100 000, 10 000 or 5 000 g.mol-1) was then experienced on microfiltration permeate. Whatever the pressure (3 and 5 bar) and the membrane, the residual turbidity was below 0.5 NTU, complying with the recommendations of the NF and RO manufacturers. Membrane FS40PP with the highest MWCO (100 000 g.mol-1) and a 3 bar pressure was preferred as it limited permeability loss during the filtration stage (41%, against 68% and 62% with membranes of 10 000 and 5 000 g.mol-1 MWCO, respectively). [SOURCE: Page_166]

Finally, the removal efficiency of this pre-treatment (sieving + microfiltration + ultrafiltration on FS40PP at VRR 3.5) reached 99% for turbidity, 50% for COD, 12% for CODdiff, 42% for TN, 40% for conductivity, 26% for OD216.4 and 49% for OD264.4. The decrease in sugar concentrations was unexpected: 56% for fructose, 98% for glucose and 100% for sucrose. This result was due to fermentation (Paramithiotis et al., 2010) during storage even if mostly at 4°C, detected by the decrease of pH and chlorine concentration, and confirmed by specific acetate and lactate peaks on HPIC chromatograms. [SOURCE: Page_166]

### 4.3.1. Critical flux, concentration polarization and fouling

All the following experiments were performed with pure water or with the pre-treated wastewater produced as described in section 4.2. Results are presented on Fig. 2, from which [SOURCE: Page_166]

________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    137 [SOURCE: Page_166]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_167]

pure water permeability Aw could be deduced according to Eq. 6 (with ∆𝜋 = 0) (Table 3). For SR3D and ESPA$_4$ membranes, Aw values before effluent filtration were similar to those in Garnier et al (2020) (Table 1), while they appeared much lower or higher respectively for NF270 (-30%) and DK (+ 45%). A small Aw decrease was observed after NF or RO treatment proving that fouling had occurred during effluent treatment. For wastewater filtration at the lowest TMP values, the relation between JP and TMP was linear, showing that no fouling had yet occurred but only a reversible concentration polarization phenomenon (eq. 8) (Aimar, 2006). Above a given flux value, named the critical flux, it was no longer linear meaning that irreversible concentration polarization occurred together with a likely irreversible fouling (Aimar et al., 2010). The critical flux and corresponding pressure obtained graphically (Table 4) show that membranes do not differ from each other on these parameters but rather on AW level (Table 3). To confirm the fouling phenomenon, JP was studied over time and compared with initial pure water flux: for each TMP applied up to 15 bar, flux measurements were made after 5 min (initial flux) and 30 min; for 25 bar, it was after 5, 15 and 30 min. TMP was then decreased (20, 15, 10, 5 and 1 bar) and a measurement was made after 10-min run. As shown in Fig. 2, during pressure increase and below the critical flux, the steady state was quickly reached as the permeate flux was almost the same after 5 and 30 min. On the contrary, for NF270 membrane and above the critical flux, a decrease of up to 10% of Jp was observed over time (Fig. 2a). Moreover, hysteresis appeared for all membranes when TMP was decreased, confirming that critical flux had been exceeded and that fouling had developed (Aimar et al., 2010). [SOURCE: Page_167]

### 4.3.2. Solutes rejections

The rejection performances of the membranes were compared before and after the critical flux as both concentration polarization and fouling might have beneficial or detrimental impact on membrane selectivity (Aimar et al., 2010). Rejections of COD, glucose and fructose versus permeate flux are given Fig. 3. After pre-treatment, sucrose concentrations were below the quantification limit and were not considered. As expected, RO gave the highest rejections. For NF, rejections decreased with MWCO increase (Table 1), assessing that size exclusion was the major mechanism for NF membranes. DK and NF270 showed comparable patterns. [SOURCE: Page_168]

The COD rejections for DK (150–300 g.mol-1), NF270 (150–300 g.mol-1), SR3D (200 g.mol-1) and ESPA$_4$ (99.2% NaCl) membranes increased with TMP from 74.6% to 81.8%, 76.6% to 83.6%, 53.2% to 74.5% and 90.3% to 95.2%, respectively (Fig. 3-a). At 25 bar, the minimal COD values in the permeate remained high for NF (above 700 mg O$_2$.L-1), and much lower for ESPA$_4$ (208 mg O$_2$.L-1). COD rejections continually increased but more and more slowly showing that exceeding the critical flux (between 90 and 100 L. h-1.m-²) is not efficient. For fructose and glucose (87–89% and 11–13% of total sugars in the retentate, respectively) the [SOURCE: Page_168]

________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    139 [SOURCE: Page_168]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_169]

same membrane ranking was observed (Fig. 3-b). The rejections were at least 95% for NF270, 91% for DK and 98% for ESPA$_4$ membrane which was consistent with other studies on sugars (Garnier et al., 2020; N. Nguyen et al., 2015). Low rejection (58 to 86%) was observed for SR3D confirming a different behaviour, as already noticed on carrot processing wastewater for protons, amino-acid-type and bicarbonates (Garnier et al., 2020). CODdiff rejection was always lower than the COD rejection (Fig. 3-a) which suggested that organic non-sugar molecules showed poor rejection. To investigate this, the rejections of TN, OD216.4 and OD264.4 were examined and compared with that for COD and CODdiff (Fig. 4) Results for NF270 membrane were not presented, as it behaves like DK membrane. [SOURCE: Page_169]

OD216.4 rejections were below COD rejections for SR3D (200 g.mol-1), similar for NF270 and DK (150–300 g.mol-1) and above for ESPA$_4$ membrane. This suggests that size exclusion was the main selectivity factor and that OD216.4 represents non-aromatic and non-sugar molecules with molecular weight below 150 g.mol-1 (Fig. 4). For ESPA$_4$ membrane (RO), OD216.4, OD264.4 and TN rejections were above CODdiff rejection suggesting that small and undetermined molecules migrate through the membrane (Fig. 4-c). For all membranes, OD264.4 rejections were similar and slightly above TN rejections suggesting that the main part of nitrogen compounds detected by TN measurements absorb at 264.4 nm and would thus contain aromatic amino acids identified in cauliflower (Table 5). OD264.4 rejections of SR3D, NF270 and DK membranes were respectively between 65.0% and 80.9%, 89% and 91.7% and 87.8% and 90.1%, consistent with MW of those aromatic amino acids and MWCO of the membranes. They appeared to be better rejected by ESPA$_4$ membrane, with OD264.4 rejections between 96.8% and 100%. OD216.4 rejections were always below OD264.4 and TN rejections, showing that non-aromatic amino acids partially transfer through NF membranes, probably due to smaller MW. [SOURCE: Page_169]

### 4.3.3. Minerals rejection

Rejections of sulphate and magnesium for NF270 and DK membranes were consistent with manufacturer data (Table 6). Differences can be due to operating concentrations and pressures, or to model solutions (and not complex effluents) used by manufacturers. Again, different behaviour of SR3D was observed with sulphate rejection (69.7% instead of 99%). For all ions (Table 7), this membrane generally gave lower rejections than other NF membranes (NF270 and DK ). [SOURCE: Page_171]

Ionic mass balances were established for the retentate and the permeate for DK and ESPA$_4$ (Table 7) and ESPA$_4$ (Table 8), both at 19 bar. As in Garnier et al. (2020), for both membranes the sum of the negative charges was far lower than the positive ones, especially in the retentate and with DK. This difference can be explained by the presence of small negatively charged molecules at the pH of the pre-treated effluent (pH 4.7), such as amino acids (Table 5) or organic acids (lactic acid, pKa 3.86) that were detected but not quantified in the effluent. Consequently, cations appeared globally more retained than anions in the case of the DK membrane, which can be an artifact of this proportion of negative ions not quantified in the retentate. Moreover, for two ions with the same charge but different radii, the one having the highest charge density would exhibit the highest rejection (Epsztein, Shaulsky, Dizge, Warsinger, & Elimelech, 2018). This may explain the highest rejection of Cl- as compared to NO$_3$-, or that of Na+ as compared to NH$_4$+, due to their respective ionic radii (Lide, 2004; R. D. Shannon, 1976). Far more H2PO$_4$- is rejected due to its higher molecular weight (MW = 98 g.mol-1). ESPA$_4$ led to the best rejections, at about 100% for divalent ions and above 95% for monovalent ones provided pressure was above 10 bar (or Jp above 40 L.h-1.m-2). [SOURCE: Page_173]

### 4.3.4. Choice of NF or RO membranes for the reconditioning treatment

Comparable results were observed with NF270 and DK membranes and lower performance (lower rejections) with SR3D membrane. NF270 at TMP = 15 bar and DK at TMP = 19 bar (pressure at critical flux) appeared as the best compromises for COD rejection and permeate flux. With RO membrane (ESPA4), the rejections were higher and critical flux corresponded to TMP = 24 bar (Table 4). To obtain the best compromise between COD rejection and permeate flux and to ensure a residual COD in the permeate below 400 mg O2.L-1, ESPA4 membrane was selected at about 19 bar. The permeate quality indicators are summarized in Table 8. For an equivalent permeate flux, the ESPA4 treatment of complex carrot peeling effluent at about 15 bar had allowed a better permeate quality (Garnier et al., 2020). This can be explained by the much lower organic load of the carrots processing wastewater (Table 9), similar rejections leading to lower concentrations in the permeate. A additional explanation may be a higher fermentation of sugar due to longer storage in the case of cauliflower processing wastewater, leading to an increase in small metabolites content such as acetic or lactic acids, which can permeate through the membrane. ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                     145 [SOURCE: Page_174]

Chapitre III : Sélection des prétraitements et du procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_178]

5. Conclusion A complex cauliflower processing wastewater resulting from blanching was treated using membrane processes, in order to produce water of a quality high enough to be reused inside the factory. The adopted pre-treatment consisted in a double sieving step at 169 µm and 79 µm followed by a 100 000 g.mol-1 MWCO ultrafiltration. Its removal efficiency reached 99% for turbidity, 50% for COD and 40% for conductivity especially. At industrial scale, this pre- treatment could be replaced by a single submerged hollow fibre ultrafiltration (Nelson et al., 2007). RO treatment with ESPA$_4$ membrane was then necessary to reach the best permeate quality. It was optimized at 19 bar, leading to a residual COD value in the permeate of 225 mg O$_2$.L-1 due to the transfer of small non-aromatic compounds. Solution-Diffusion model and film model theory were applicable to describe glucose and fructose transfer, for DK, NF270 and ESPA$_4$ membranes. Permeability coefficient Bi obtained for glucose and fructose was similar (0.45 x 10-6 m.s-1) and consistent with values calculated from other studies (0.25 to 0.95 x 10-6 m.s-1regardless of the concentration of glucose in the feed solution and its composition. These results, if industrially confirmed, open the possibility of water recycling of cauliflower blanching wastewater. However, it would be necessary to investigate long-term accumulation of the residual solutes in the recycled effluent. A Life Cycle Assessment on the plant under study confirmed that this wastewater recycling through UF plus RO treatment was beneficial. It offers a way to limit the reliance on water resource and to face water restrictions that in certain regions lead to stop or delay food plants production. [SOURCE: Page_178]

[SOURCE: Page_178]

5. Conclusion du chapitre III Ce chapitre a permis : d’identifier les données manquantes (point 1 de la méthodologie générale), d’identifier les paramètres clés (point 2 de la méthodologie / Outil D), de définir sur cette base un schéma de procédé (point 3 de la méthodologie / Outil E), d’identifier des modèles de dimensionnement (point 4 de la méthodologie) et de valider le schéma de procédé à l’échelle du laboratoire (point 5 de la méthodologie). Il a aussi permis de sélectionner le meilleur prétraitement et la meilleure membrane à tester sur le pilote semi-industriel (Chapitre IV). [SOURCE: Page_180]

La première difficulté a été de connaître la composition des effluents et d’identifier les « paramètres clés » (composés à éliminer par le procédé de traitement) pour compléter l’Outil D définit au chapitre I, paragraphe 1. En effet, les seules informations disponibles étaient que l’effluent contenait un mélange d’eau, des molécules issues du légume concerné et des produits de décomposition de ces légumes. Des analyses globales des effluents ont d’abord permis d’identifier les paramètres clés globaux des effluents : les MES, la turbidité, la DCO, la conductivité et l’azote total. Ensuite, en observant l’évolution de ces paramètres clés globaux lors du traitement membranaire mais aussi en analysant la composition des légumes, d’autres paramètres clés plus spécifiques ont pu être identifiés : le glucose, le fructose et le saccharose dont la présence risque de générer un développement bactérien, non acceptable sur l’unité de production mais aussi de l’acide lactique (Garnier, 2021). [SOURCE: Page_180]

Plusieurs prétraitements ont été testés et un tamisage à 169 µm puis 79 µm suivi d’une ultrafiltration (MWCO=15 000 g.mol-1) à 3 bar ont été retenus pour les essais sur le pilote semi-industriel. A l’échelle industrielle, cette étape de prétraitement pourra être remplacée par un tamis rotatif avec un seuil de coupure de 1 ou 2 mm suivi d’un système équipé de membranes immergées planes ou fibres creuses comme dans l’étude réalisée par Nelson et al. (2007) sur un site industriel produisant des légumes frais coupés (Nelson et al., 2007). Des expériences ont été réalisées sur le pilote de laboratoire (filtration membranaire) et l’influence de la PTM a été étudiée. L’OI et plus spécifiquement la membrane ESPA$_4$ a montré de meilleures performances de traitement (compromis entre des bons Tr en DCO et sucres et de bons Jp). Le modèle de SD avec prise en compte du phénomène de polarisation de concentration a permis de modéliser les phénomènes de transfert (Publication 3, paragraphe 4.4) et de définir des premiers paramètres de dimensionnement tels que la perméabilité à l’eau, les perméabilités de la membrane au glucose et au fructose et les coefficients de transfert dans la couche limite de polarisation correspondant. [SOURCE: Page_180]

Dans le cadre de ce chapitre, j’ai aussi mis en évidence deux phénomènes qui modifient les performances du traitement : une dégradation par fermentation des effluents et un phénomène d’adsorption sur les membranes. En effet, la fermentation va produire de petites molécules qui vont plus facilement traverser la membrane et l’adsorption en modifiant les caractéristiques de la membrane (charge, groupes fonctionnelles…) va modifier les densités de flux des solutés (Ji) et d’eau (Jw) à travers la membrane. ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    151 [SOURCE: Page_180]

Chapitre IV : Optimisation du traitement par procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_184]

Ce chapitre présente les résultats obtenus sur le pilote semi-industriel et propose un premier dimensionnement de l’installation de recyclage. Il a plusieurs objectifs :  Valider à l’échelle semi-industrielle le schéma de procédé envisagé à l’échelle laboratoire (point 5 de la méthodologie générale),  Identifier les meilleures conditions opératoires à mettre en œuvre,  Proposer une solution de recyclage et une intégration industrielle. [SOURCE: Page_184]

Pour cela, plusieurs séries d’expériences ont été réalisées en faisant varier soit le débit d’alimentation (Fe) via le débit du rétentat (Fr), soit la PTM ou soit le FRV. [SOURCE: Page_184]

1. Caractérisation des effluents en amont de l’OI Les effluents bruts (CaR, CaB et ChB) , dont les caractéristiques sont données au paragraphe 2 du chapitre III (2ème série d’analyses des Tableau III-1, Tableau III-2 et Tableau III-3, chapitre III, paragraphe 2), ont été prétraités puis traités par OI. Compte tenu de la durée des expériences, les étapes de prétraitement et de traitement par OI ont été effectuées sur 2 jours séparés. Une étape de stockage soit à 4°C soit à -18°C a donc eu lieu entre ces 2 étapes. Comme une dégradation des effluents a été précédemment observée lors de ce stockage, il est donc important de refaire une caractérisation très précise des 3 effluents prétraités après stockage et juste en amont du traitement par OI (prélèvement dans la cuve avant mise en route du pilote). [SOURCE: Page_184]

1.1.       Effluent issu du rinçage après pelage de la carotte (CaR) Les qualités de l’effluent CaR brut (Tableau III-1, chapitre III, paragraphe 2) et avant l’étape d’OI (Tableau IV-1) ont été comparées. La proportion de sucres (non retenus par les prétraitements) dans la DCO augmente après les prétraitements (Figure IV-1). Cela s’explique par l’élimination de pelure et de macromolécules, « non sucres ». [SOURCE: Page_184]

Le fructose reste le sucre majoritairement présent suivi du glucose. Par contre, les concentrations des différents sucres varient : les concentrations en glucose et fructose augmentent en passant respectivement de 349-493 mg.L-1 à 492-581 mg.L-1 et de 563-725 mg.L-1 à 713-893 mg.L-1 et les concentrations en saccharose diminuent de 47-171 mg.L-1 à 52-64 mg.L-1 (Tableau III-1, chapitre III, paragraphe 2 et Tableau IV-1). Une hypothèse avancée est l’hydrolyse acide du saccharose en glucose et fructose pendant les mises à température de l’effluent ainsi que pendant l’étape d’UF. Les bilans matières (équations, Figure I-6, chapitre I, paragraphe 2.1) réalisées pendant le prétraitement par UF montrent, en effet, une disparition du glucose (-25% sur la 1er série d’UF et -5% sur la 2ème série d’UF) et du fructose (-37% sur la 1er série d’UF et -6% sur la 2ème série d’UF) et une apparition du saccharose (+49% sur la 1er série d’UF et +24% sur la 2ème série d’UF). [SOURCE: Page_184]

________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                    155 [SOURCE: Page_184]

Chapitre IV : Optimisation du traitement par procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_185]

Les acides organiques étant partiellement dissociés, il est possible de les détecter sur le chromatogramme « anions » obtenu par HPIC groupés autour d’un pic à 3,2 minutes. L’aire obtenue de ce pic pour l’effluent brut est de 5,3 et passe à 1,8 pour l’effluent après prétraitement et en amont d’OI. Une hypothèse avancée est la dégradation des acides organiques sans doute liée à un développement bactérien, notamment en éthanol (Di Cagno, Coda, De Angelis, & Gobbetti, 2013). [SOURCE: Page_185]

Pour cet effluent, 3 séries d’expérience ont été réalisées pour optimiser le traitement par OI (effets de Fr, PTM et FRV). La caractérisation de l’effluent en amont de chacune des expériences a été effectuée (Tableau IV-1). Les valeurs des différents paramètres de l’effuent sont similaires sauf pour la conductivité qui passe de 779,0 µS.cm-1 pour la 1ère série d’expérience à 925 µS.cm-1 pour la 3ème série d’expérience (+19%) et pour la turbidité qui en passant de 0,4 NTU à 5,6 NTU est multipliée par 14. Cela s’explique par le mode opératoire. En effet, et pour avoir suffisamment de volume pour réaliser la 3ème série d’expérience (variation du FRV), les effluents utilisés lors de la 2ème série d’expérience (variation de la PTM) ont été réutilisés et ont représenté 45% du volume total de l’effluent utilisé lors de la 3ème série d’expérience. Enfin, la concentration en azote totale en amont de l’OI étant faible (entre 4 et 5 mg N.L-1), il a été décidé de ne pas suivre ce paramètre dans la suite de l’étude. [SOURCE: Page_185]

Figure IV-1 : Proportion de sucres (% de la DCO) de l’effluent CaR dans les effluents bruts et en amont du traitement par OI [SOURCE: Page_185]

1.2.        Effluent issu du blanchiment de la carotte (CaB) Concernant l’effluent CaB, entre l’effluent brut (Tableau III-2, chapitre III, paragraphe 2) et l’effluent en amont de l’OI (Tableau IV-2), une baisse de la DCO est observée ; elle passe de 5 633 mg O$_2$.L-1 à 4 900 mg O$_2$.L-1 mais sans impact sur la proportion de sucres dans la DCO [SOURCE: Page_186]

Chapitre IV : Optimisation du traitement par procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_187]

(Figure IV-2). Dans cet effluent qui contenait beaucoup moins de MES que l’effluent CaR, les concentrations en glucose et fructose baissent et passent respectivement de 552 mg.L-1 à 472 mg.L-1 (-14%) et de 983 mg.L-1 à 787 mg.L-1 (-20%) alors que la concentration en saccharose reste stable en passant de 1 660 mg.L-1 à 1600 mg.L-1 (-4%). Une hypothèse pour justifier ces trois baisses peut être une adsorption et une dégradation des sucres sur la membrane d’UF. En effet, les bilans matières (équations, Figure I-6, chapitre I, paragraphe 2.1) lors de l’UF montrent des baisses de 10% en fructose, 8% en glucose et 11% en saccharose et une hausse de 50% de l’aire du pic obtenues par HPIC et correspondant aux trois acides organiques (acide lactique, acide formique et acide acétique). Aucune diminution n’avait été observée sur le prétraitement par MF en amont des expériences sur le pilote de laboratoire. La différence de comportement des effluents CaR et CaB peut s’expliquer par le mode opératoire. En effet, l’effluent CaB a été prétraité par UF après l’effluent CaR alors qu’ils ont été décongelés en même temps. Une dégradation plus importante de l’effluent CaB a donc eu lieu. La DCO de l’effluent CaB (4 900 mg O$_2$.L-1) comme les teneurs en azote totale (32,9 mg N.L-1) et en saccharose (1 600 mg.L-1) sont plus élévées que celles de l’effluent CaR (DCO=2 500-2 800 mg O$_2$.L-1, Azote totale=4-5 mg N.L-1, Saccharose=52-64 mg.L-1). Cela peut s’expliquer par la température de l’effluent en sortie de l’unité de production qui est beaucoup plus élevée pour l’efffluent issu du blanchiment (64-71°C) que pour l’effluent issu du rinçage après pelage (31°C) et donc plus favorable à la dissolution des composés de la carotte. Les concentrations en glucose et fructose qui étaient supérieures dans l’effluent CaB brut pour rapport à l’effluent CaR (dues probablement a une dissolution plus importante) ont maintenant une concentration similaire dans les effluents en amont de l’OI (augmentation de la proportion de sucres observée pour l’effluent CaR). Concernant les ions, des concentrations similaires sont mesurées sauf pour le Na+ et le K+ (1,5 à 2 fois supérieures dans l’effluent CaB). [SOURCE: Page_187]

Chapitre IV : Optimisation du traitement par procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_189]

De la même façon que pour l’effluent CaR, 3 séries d’expérience de traitement par OI ont été réalisées. Alors que pour l’effluent CaR, les teneurs en sucres étaient similaires pour les 3 séries d’expérience, on observe des concentrations en saccharose et en glucose plus élevées dans l’effluent utilisé pour la 1ère série d’expériences (variation de Fr). En effet, les concentrations en glucose et saccharose qui sont respectivement égales à 867 mg.L-1 et 79 mg.L-1 dans l’effluent de la 1ère série d’expérience passent à 139 mg.L-1 (-84%) et 204 mg.L-1 (-76%) pour le glucose et 17 mg.L-1 (-78%) et 2 mg.L-1 (-97%) pour le saccharose dans les effluents des 2ème et 3ème séries d’expérience (Tableau IV-3). Le fructose quant à lui n’est pas affecté. Une dégradation des sucres et ici principalement du glucose et du saccharose (plus fermentescibles) se produit. Cette dégradation est confirmée par l’augmentation de l’aire du pic obtenue par HPIC qui correspond aux trois acides organiques (acide lactique, acide formique et acide acétique) qui est de 4,9 pour la première série d’expérience et respectivement 6,4 (+31%) et 5,8 (+18%) pour les 2 autres séries d’expérience. Enfin, la concentration en saccharose en amont de l’OI étant faible, les résultats concernant ce sucre n’ont pas pu être analysés dans la suite de l’étude. [SOURCE: Page_189]

2. Phénomènes d’adsorption sur la membrane ESPA$_4$ De précédentes études dans le laboratoire ont mis en évidence un phénomène d’adsorption des sucres et des acides organiques sur les membranes de NF et d’OI (Fargues, Sagne, Szymczyk, Fievet, & Lameloise, 2013; N. Nguyen et al., 2016; N. D. T. N. Nguyen, 2014; Sagne, 2008; Sagne et al., 2008). Dans le cadre de ces études, des isothermes d’adsorption des molécules seules, des molécules en mélanges ou d’effluents industriels ont été établies soit dans des réacteurs fermés agités soit lors d’expériences sur le pilote semi-industriel. Les résultats montrent que ces phénomènes d’adsorption induisent des modifications des propriétés physico-chimiques des membranes : modification de la charge et de hydrophobicité notamment (Sagne, 2008) mais que, dans une configuration industrielle en fonctionnement continu, un état d’équilibre va être atteint (N. Nguyen et al., 2016; N. D. T. N. Nguyen, 2014). Dans le cadre de cette thèse, j’ai travaillé sur plusieurs effluents industriels dont la composition varie au cours du temps (fonctionnement discontinu du procédé industriel). Cela signifie que j’ai une multitude de molécules qui sont en compétition pour s’adsorber sur la membrane et que les équilibres et donc les performances du procédé vont être modifiées au cours du temps. [SOURCE: Page_191]

Je me suis donc fixé 3 objectifs pour cette thèse :  Identifier la nature de plusieurs molécules venant s’adsorber sur la membrane,  Etudier l’impact de cette adsorption sur Jp,  Etudier l’impact de cette adsorption sur les taux de rétention des sucres (chapitre IV, paragraphe 3). [SOURCE: Page_191]

Les tableaux en annexe IV.1 (Tableau A IV-1, Tableau A IV-2, Tableau A IV-3, Tableau A IV-4 et Tableau A IV-5) résument les baisses de concentration de chaque paramètre / soluté après mise en contact pendant 30 min à PTM=0 bar des différents effluents (3 effluents industriels [SOURCE: Page_191]

Chapitre IV : Optimisation du traitement par procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_192]

et pour les 2 solutions « modèle ») avec la membrane ESPA$_4$. A noter que comme les volumes d’effluent utilisés et les pH de ces effluents sont différents d’une mise en contact à une autre, cela n’a pas de sens de comparer entre eux les pourcentages d’un même paramètre. Par exemple, entre un pH de 5 ou de 6, les proportions des formes acide et basique des acides organiques vont varier, cela va modifier l’affinité avec la membrane et donc les quantités adsorbées. [SOURCE: Page_192]

Plusieurs hypothèses ont été avancées pour expliquer les baisses de concentration observées : une adsorption sur la membrane, une dégradation par fermentation ou encore un phénomène de dilution dans le volume mort du pilote. Le Tableau IV-5 présente les disparitions en glucose et en fructose lors de la mise en contact de l’effluent CaR et de la solution « modèle sucres » sur le module ESPA$_4$ installé sur le pilote semi-industriel. D’abord, aucune évolution significative des concentrations dans la cuve n’a été observée pendant 1h^30 (minimum). Pour la solution « modèle » et sur cette durée, les concentrations étaient pour le glucose de 294 ± 12 mg.L-1 et pour le fructose de 502 ± 20 mg.L-1 alors que pour l’effluent CaR, elles étaient de 443 ± 18 mg.L-1 pour le glucose et de 659 ± 26 mg.L-1 pour le fructose. L’hypothèse d’une dégradation de l’effluent par fermentation semble peu donc probable. Par ailleurs, si la disparition des sucres était intégralement due au volume mort, celui-ci serait de 4,5 L environ (10 - 10 x 435 mg.L-1 / 297 mg.L-1), ce qui semble très important car le pilote a été intégralement vidangé avant l’expérience. De plus et dans cette hypothèse, les baisses (en %) de l’ensemble des solutés présentes dans l’effluent CaR seraient les mêmes, ce que l’on ne retrouve pas (Tableau A IV-2 en annexe IV.1) ; la disparition de la DCO est, par exemple, entre 12 et 20% alors que la disparition de glucose est entre 2 et 11%. Les hypothèses d’une dilution partielle de l’effluent dans le volume mort du pilote et d’un phénomène d’adsorption sur la membrane sont donc privilégiées. [SOURCE: Page_192]

Tableau IV-5 : Disparition du glucose et du fructose lors des essais sur le pilote semi- industriel (en amont de l’expérience avec variation de la PTM, PTM= 0 bar, Fr=450 L.h-1) Concentration      Concentration        Quantité             Concentration au avant mise en       après mise en       disparue               bout d’1h^30 -1                  -1 contact (mg.L )    contact (mg.L )        (g.m-2)           d’expérience (mg.L-1) Solution « modèle » - Volume de l’effluent mis en contact : 10 L Glucose         435 ± 17            297 ± 12             0,7                     289 ± 12 Fructose        717 ± 29            502 ± 20             1,2                     499 ± 20 Effluent CaR – Volume de l’effluent mis en contact : 27,6 L Glucose         492 ± 20            436 ± 17             0,8                     450 ± 18 Fructose        713 ± 29            645 ± 26             1,0                     679 ± 27 [SOURCE: Page_192]

Pour l’ensemble des effluents, les résultats montrent que tous les paramètres, molécules (sucres et acides aminés) et ions analysés disparaissent après mise en contact avec la ________________________________________________________________________________________________ Recyclage d’eau au sein des industries agro-alimentaires                                     163 [SOURCE: Page_192]

Chapitre IV : Optimisation du traitement par procédé membranaire ________________________________________________________________________________________________ [SOURCE: Page_193]

membrane mais dans des proportions variables. Les différents acides aminés présents en concentrations égales et faibles dans la solution « modèle acides aminés » disparaissent dans des proportions équivalentes sauf éventuellement l’alanine qui disparait en quantité légérement supérieure. Ce qui semble confirmer l’adsorption de cet acide aminé. De la même manière, les différents sucres (glucose, fructose, saccharose) présents en concentrations différentes et proches de l’effluent CaR dans la solution « modèle sucres » disparaissent dans des proportions équivalentes. Ce n’est plus le cas dans les effluents industriels. En effet et par exemple pour l’effluent CaR, la proportion de saccharose qui disparait est plus importante que pour les 2 autres sucres. A noter que comme pour le glucose et le fructose, l’hypothèse d’une dégradation du saccharose est exclue car sa concentration reste stable dans la cuve et égale à 53 ± 3 mg.L-1 pendant 1h^30 (minimum). Concernant le spectre UV, les composés détectés à 264,4 et 292,6 nm (représentant des molécules aromatiques) et ceux détectés à 321,2 nm (représentant des composés phénoliques) disparaissent dans des proportions plus importantes que ceux détectés à 216,4 nm (liaisons peptidiques). Cette disparition peut s’expliquer par un phénomène d’adsorption car des études précédentes (Fargues et al., 2013; Sagne et al., 2008) ont montrées que les molécules aromatiques et les cycles phénoliques s’absorbent mieux sur la membrane. Concernant les ions et suivant la nature de l’effluent, les anions disparaissent soit plus (effluent CaR), soit moins que les cations (effluent CaB) ou soit dans les mêmes proportions que les cations (effluent ChB). La charge de la membrane étant généralement négative pour les membranes d’OI (Norberg, Hong, Taylor, & Zhao, 2007) et en l’absence d’autres molécules, on pourrait s’attendre à une adsorption plus importante des cations. Or, des molécules non identifiées et chargées négativement sont présentes dans l’effluent (paragraphe 3.7 de la Publication 2 et paragraphe 4.3.3 de la Publication 3). Les hypothèses avancées sont que ces molécules chargées négativement rentrent en compétition avec les anions modifient les équilibres d’adsorption et le point iso-électrique de la membrane (Aimar et al., 2010). [SOURCE: Page_193]

La valeur de Jp et donc la perméabilité de la membrane sont affectées par l’adsorption des molécules (Eq I-10). Camille SAGNE indique dans sa thèse que Jp diminue d’autant plus que la solution traitée contient un grand nombre de molécules (Sagne, 2008) et le justifie par une adsorption coopérative sur la membrane. Zhang et al. ont, en effet, montré que les adsorptions de 2 solutés (le phénol et l’aniline) dans un système binaire était remarquablement plus élevé que celles mesurées dans un système avec une seul molécule à la même concentration due à des interactions entre les 2 solutés (Zhang et al., 2007). Cette hypothèse semble se vérifier lorsque je calcule la baisse de la valeur de perméabilité et donc celle de Jp (Figure A IV-1 en annexe IV.1). En effet, pour les 2 solutions modèles qui contiennent un nombre limité de molécules, les pertes de perméabilité sont dans l’intervalle d’incertitude de la mesure (Tableau IV-6). Pour l’effluent CaR, la perte de perméabilité reste négligeable (5%). Par contre, pour l’effluent ChB, elle est significative (13%) et probablement [SOURCE: Page_193]

due à une plus grande variété de molécules générées par le traitement thermique du chou- fleur lors de l’opération de blanchiment. Une autre hypothèse pour justifier ces différences est la concentration des effluents. En effet, l’effluent ChB a une DCO 2 fois supérieure à celle de l’effluent CaR. Or, plus Cr,i est élevé, plus Δπ est élevé (Eq I-16) et plus Jw est faible (Eq I-19 et I-22). Par ailleurs et pour la solution « modèle acides aminés », les concentrations en acides aminés étaient très faibles, peu de sites d’adsortion ont probablement été occupés. [SOURCE: Page_194]
